one_liner: A professional, membership-based podcast and video content studio in Tel Aviv.

overview.problem: Video podcasting has exploded, but Tel Aviv has no dedicated paid studio -- only a free promotional space tied to a marketing company.
overview.solution: A membership and hourly-rental video/podcast studio with professional equipment, following a business format already proven and sellable in US markets.
overview.edge: Confirmed absence of a paid dedicated studio locally, plus real proof of demand from adjacent creative-space marketplaces that don't themselves operate one.

sections.heading: 1. Problem & Market Opportunity
sections.body:
Video podcasting has moved from a niche production choice to the default expectation in barely two years. YouTube users streamed over 700 million hours of video podcasts on connected TVs in October 2025, nearly double the 400 million hours logged a year earlier [1] -- a growth rate that outpaces almost every other content format tracked by the platform. More than 70% of active podcasters now shoot video alongside audio, and 53% of US podcast consumers say they now prefer watching to simply listening, according to industry survey data [1]. This is not a temporary pandemic-era spike; it reflects a structural shift in how platforms reward and distribute audio content, with YouTube, Spotify, and TikTok all now actively favoring video-native podcast formats in their recommendation algorithms.

Producing video podcast content at a professional level is materially harder than producing audio alone. It requires multi-camera setups, controlled lighting, acoustic treatment, and either in-house editing skill or a paid post-production relationship -- a combination most individual creators, early-stage founders, and small businesses in Tel Aviv do not have access to and cannot justify building in-house for occasional use. The natural response to unmet infrastructure demand is a rental studio model, and this format is already proven and commercially viable in other markets: multiple independently-owned turn-key podcast studio rental businesses operate successfully across Los Angeles, Nashville, and other major US creator hubs, with several actively listed for sale as going concerns [3], confirming the underlying unit economics work as a standalone small business, not merely as a marketing loss-leader for something else.

In Tel Aviv specifically, direct research turned up exactly one comparable option: a free recording studio opened in 2022 by ThoughtLeaders, an influencer-marketing agency, offered as a client-acquisition perk rather than a dedicated, reliably available commercial service [2]. No paid, professionally-equipped, purpose-built studio serving the city's active creator and startup community currently exists. Given Tel Aviv's dense concentration of startups, media professionals, and content creators, and given that the underlying demand signal (video podcast growth) is global and not US-specific, this represents a genuine, currently unclaimed local market gap rather than an assumption.

sections.heading: 2. Solution & Product
sections.body:
Cue is a membership-and-hourly-rental video and podcast production studio, offering professional multi-camera recording equipment, controlled lighting and acoustic treatment, and optional light production support (basic editing, additional camera operation) as an add-on service. The core offering is physical studio access and equipment, not a media company or content studio in the creative-agency sense -- customers bring their own concept and hosts, and Cue provides the infrastructure and technical support to produce it at a professional standard without requiring them to own equipment or hire a dedicated crew.

The facility is designed around two primary customer segments observed in the research: individual and small-team podcasters who need periodic access to professional equipment without the capital cost of owning it, and startups or small businesses producing recurring video content (founder interviews, product walkthroughs, internal training video, investor updates) who need a reliable, bookable space rather than an ad hoc arrangement. Both segments are underserved by the current Tel Aviv market, where the only comparable resource is unpredictable in availability and tied to a specific marketing agency's client relationships rather than open to the market generally.

Operationally, the format itself is de-risked by precedent rather than novel: the business model of a dedicated, professionally-equipped rental studio already works as a standalone commercial venture in multiple US markets, evidenced by active listings of comparable businesses for sale [3], which provides real reference points for staffing structure, equipment specification, and pricing approach rather than requiring the model to be proven from first principles. What has not yet been established is a dedicated version of this format in Tel Aviv or, more broadly, in Israel -- the opportunity is in bringing an already-validated operating model to a market that has real, growing demand for it and no existing paid provider.

The studio itself would launch as a single flagship location rather than attempting multiple sites immediately, allowing real booking and retention data to validate demand before any expansion decision, consistent with how comparable US operators appear to have scaled based on available business-for-sale documentation [3].

sections.heading: 3. Business Model
sections.body:
Revenue follows standard bar/lounge-adjacent rental economics familiar from comparable service businesses: a combination of hourly walk-in bookings and a discounted monthly membership tier, with production add-ons as a secondary revenue line. Pricing has to be anchored against what creators are already accustomed to paying elsewhere, since the target customer has real alternatives (a marketplace-listed space, a competitor's future entry, or simply continuing without professional equipment) rather than a captive need.

Comparable production and creative space listings on marketplaces such as PeerSpace, which has raised over $40M and operates across major cities including Los Angeles, New York, London, Paris, and Sydney [4], typically price professional-grade recording and production spaces in a broad range depending on equipment tier and city cost base. Anchoring Cue's walk-in rate at NIS 250/hour (roughly $70) reflects a professional-but-accessible position within that broader marketplace range, rather than the premium end, since Tel Aviv's creator economy is smaller and more price-sensitive than Cue's largest comparable markets. A membership tier at NIS 990/month (about $275) for 6 hours of studio time, with discounted additional hours and priority booking, is anchored below the cost of booking 6 hours a la carte -- the standard mechanic used to convert occasional users into predictable recurring revenue, structured so a customer using the studio more than roughly twice a month is clearly better off on membership.

Secondary revenue comes from production add-ons -- basic editing, an additional camera operator, or graphics/lower-thirds work -- billed per project rather than bundled into the base rate, since these are optional and usage varies significantly by customer sophistication. A smaller but real revenue line exists in private event or workshop bookings during off-peak daytime hours, when the studio would otherwise sit idle.

Critically, these prices are a starting hypothesis to be tested against real booking behavior in the studio's first 90 days of operation, not a fixed assumption -- both the walk-in rate and the membership discount ratio should be revisited once actual demand elasticity is observed, since no directly comparable Israeli pricing data currently exists to calibrate against in advance.

sections.heading: 4. Go-to-Market
sections.body:
The launch strategy centers on a single flagship studio placed in a Tel Aviv neighborhood with high existing density of startups, media professionals, and independent creators, rather than a more generic or lower-cost location -- proximity to the target customer's daily routine matters more for a rental-by-the-hour business than proximity to general foot traffic, since bookings are planned in advance rather than impulse-driven.

Pre-launch marketing should target the specific, identifiable community of active local podcasters and video creators directly, since this is a small enough population in Tel Aviv to reach through direct outreach rather than broad advertising -- through existing podcast-focused Facebook and WhatsApp groups, direct outreach to hosts of shows already known to be active, and partnerships with the handful of startup accelerators and coworking spaces that already have relationships with the target customer base. A direct comparison to ThoughtLeaders' free offering is a deliberate part of the pitch, not something to avoid: positioning Cue explicitly as the reliable, professional-grade paid alternative to an inconsistent free option gives early customers a clear reason to switch rather than asking them to adopt an entirely new behavior.

A soft-launch period of four to six weeks, offering discounted or complimentary sessions to a curated group of known local creators in exchange for reviews, testimonials, and word-of-mouth referral, builds a credible base of social proof before the studio opens to the general public at full pricing. This mirrors how comparable US studio businesses appear to have built initial bookings, based on available public information about how similar operators describe their launch approach [3].

Listing the studio on creative-space marketplaces such as Splacer, which already has real reach and trust within Israel's event and meeting-space rental market, functions as a secondary discovery channel once the studio is operational -- not a primary launch strategy, since Splacer itself does not build or market studios, only lists spaces others already operate. Proving booking volume and membership retention in this single flagship location for at least two full quarters is the explicit gate before any second-location decision is made.

sections.heading: 5. Key Challenges
sections.body:
The most immediate risk is the free alternative already in the market: if ThoughtLeaders' 2022 studio is still actively operating, Cue must win on reliability, equipment quality, and professional service rather than simply existing as a paid option, since price-sensitive early-stage creators may default to a free resource even if inferior. The mitigation is direct: build the pitch and the actual customer experience explicitly around the specific gaps a marketing-agency-run free perk cannot close -- guaranteed availability, professional-grade equipment maintained to a commercial standard, and dedicated technical support during sessions -- and confirm ThoughtLeaders' current operating status directly before finalizing the launch plan, since this is a real, checkable fact rather than an assumption.

A second, structurally different risk is fast imitation once demand is proven. Splacer already has real reach and an established host network in Israel's creative and event space rental market; once Cue demonstrates that a dedicated paid studio model works in Tel Aviv, an existing Splacer host or a new entrant could list a comparable studio relatively quickly, since the barrier to entry for basic recording equipment is not high. The primary defense against this is not exclusivity of the concept but speed to a strong membership base and a reputation for service quality that a new, unproven entrant cannot immediately replicate -- membership-based recurring revenue with genuine retention is harder to displace than one-off bookings.

A longer-term, lower-probability risk worth naming honestly is a structural shift in content production itself -- if AI-generated avatars, synthetic voices, or fully virtual production become an acceptable substitute for real human-hosted video content at scale, physical studio demand could soften over a multi-year horizon. No current evidence suggests this is displacing real demand today, and the format most affected (highly produced, purely synthetic content) is a different market segment from authentic creator and founder-led video, but this is a trend worth monitoring rather than dismissing outright given how quickly the underlying technology has moved in the past two years.

sections.heading: 6. Team & Operating Plan
sections.body:
The team required to operate a single flagship studio is standard and hireable, not specialized in a way that constrains the timeline -- this is a genuine advantage relative to ideas requiring rare technical talent. Core roles needed are: a studio operations manager responsible for scheduling, customer relationships, and day-to-day facility management; a part-time or contract production support specialist handling light editing, camera operation for add-on services, and equipment maintenance; and a marketing and community lead responsible for building and maintaining relationships with the local creator and startup community that constitutes the primary customer base.

None of these roles require a background specific to podcasting or video production at an expert level -- competent hires with general audio-visual, hospitality, or small-business operations experience can be trained on the specific equipment and workflow within a normal onboarding period. This stands in contrast to ventures requiring a specific rare technical or scientific skill set, where hiring risk itself can be a material constraint on the timeline; here it is not.

Day-to-day operations follow a straightforward booking-and-turnover model familiar from comparable rental-space businesses: online scheduling, a standardized studio setup and breakdown process between bookings, and a maintenance schedule for equipment to ensure consistent quality across sessions. The operations manager role is the most important early hire, since customer experience quality in a rental-space business is disproportionately determined by how smoothly bookings, setup, and any technical troubleshooting during a session are handled -- this is the role most worth investing in finding a strong candidate for before launch, even if other roles are filled more opportunistically.

sections.heading: 7. Capital Requirements & Next Steps
sections.body:
Capital deploys in three sequential stages rather than as a single upfront commitment, allowing each stage's results to inform whether and how the next stage proceeds, consistent with SGG's general approach to staged venture funding.

Stage 1 -- Validate: approximately $25,000 over six weeks. This covers confirming ThoughtLeaders' current operating status directly, securing a specific location option (letter of intent or short-term hold on a lease rather than a signed long-term commitment), and pre-selling a small number of founding memberships to a curated group of known local creators to directly test real willingness to pay before committing to a full buildout. If founding memberships do not sell at the target rate within this window, that is a meaningful signal to revisit pricing or positioning before proceeding to Stage 2, not a reason to push forward regardless.

Stage 2 -- Launch: approximately $120,000 over three months, contingent on Stage 1 confirming real demand. This covers the full studio buildout (equipment, acoustic treatment, lighting, furnishing), initial staff hiring and training, and a 90-day operating cash runway to cover the period before booking revenue is expected to be self-sustaining.

Stage 3 -- Prove & Expand: capital sized to whatever the flagship location's actual 90-day booking volume and membership retention data supports, rather than a fixed pre-determined figure. This stage's direction -- a second Tel Aviv location, a different Israeli city, or a pause to further refine the single-location model -- should be decided based on that real operating data, not decided in advance.

The single decision gate that matters most across all three stages is membership retention in the first 90 days of full operation: does the flagship location's membership base renew at a rate that indicates a genuinely sticky recurring-revenue business, or does it require ongoing heavy customer acquisition to sustain bookings. That single metric determines whether this is a repeatable, scalable format or a single good local business, and should be the explicit go/no-go criterion before any Stage 3 capital commitment.

one_pager.subtitle: The Studio the Video-Podcast Boom Doesn't Have Yet
one_pager.overview: Cue is a membership and hourly-rental video and podcast production studio in Tel Aviv, built on a straightforward model: creators and businesses pay for professional-grade recording time instead of building their own studio. Founders, podcasters, and small businesses get multi-camera equipment, lighting, and light production support on demand; Cue owns the equipment, the space, and the booking relationship connecting them.
one_pager.thesis: Tel Aviv already has a version of this problem solved once, informally: ThoughtLeaders opened a free podcast studio in 2022 as a marketing perk. Cue takes that same proven format -- a dedicated recording space for creators -- and builds it as a real, reliable, professionally-run business rather than a promotional side project.
one_pager.opportunity: The pieces of this model are already proven elsewhere. Multiple turn-key podcast studio rental businesses operate successfully and are actively bought and sold in US markets like Los Angeles and Nashville. YouTube TV viewing hours for video podcasts nearly doubled year-over-year, and 53% of US podcast consumers now prefer watching to listening. No paid, professionally-equipped studio serving Tel Aviv's creator and startup community currently exists -- that is the whitespace Cue is built to occupy.
one_pager.strategy: Cue leads with hourly bookings and a discounted monthly membership, anchored against comparable production-space pricing on marketplaces like PeerSpace. Membership converts occasional users into predictable recurring revenue; production add-ons and off-peak private bookings provide secondary revenue on top.

who_it_serves.benefit: professional equipment without the capital cost of owning it
a reliable space for recurring video content
a real studio to list, not just another host

one_pager.current_focus: SGG Foundry is building Cue around a single flagship Tel Aviv studio: a curated launch community of known local creators, a soft-launch period to build word-of-mouth, and a direct comparison to ThoughtLeaders' free offering on reliability and equipment quality -- built to prove real booking and membership retention before any second-location decision.
one_pager.vision: SGG Foundry is building Cue with the same discipline that has taken its portfolio to a combined valuation above $400M: proving demand at a single flagship location before scaling. A $25K validation stage confirms real willingness to pay ahead of a $120K buildout once that demand is confirmed.

financials.price_unit_label: per hour (walk-in rate; membership priced separately at $275/mo for 6 hours)
financials.notes: Starting volume assumes roughly 20 booked hours/week in month 1, growing 6%/month as membership builds; variable costs cover consumables and part-time production support; fixed costs cover rent, utilities, and core staff for a single studio.
